title: 💰 The Summer Money Challenge
subtitle: 10-Week Financial Literacy + Psychological Skills
theme: Turn $50 into $500 while developing critical life skills
description: Master money management AND psychological skills! Navigate 10 weeks of financial decisions guided by Mento, your Financial Guardian. Starting with just $50, face realistic scenarios like impulse purchases, peer pressure to spend, micro-business opportunities, and investment choices. Every decision builds both financial literacy and critical psychological capabilities including delayed gratification, risk assessment, and strategic thinking.
learning_objectives: Practice delayed gratification and impulse control by choosing between immediate spending temptations and long-term financial growth
Develop risk assessment skills by evaluating micro-business ventures, savings strategies, and investment opportunities with varying risk-reward profiles
Understand core personal finance concepts including budgeting, compound growth, opportunity cost, and the difference between needs and wants
Build resilience and adaptability by navigating financial setbacks, unexpected expenses, and peer pressure to overspend
Apply strategic thinking to grow $50 into $500 over 10 weeks through a combination of saving, earning, and smart money management

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Start with $50 and navigate 10 weeks of real-world financial decisions
Each week presents a new money scenario -- read it carefully and choose your response
Your choices affect your savings, spending habits, and psychological skill scores
Build skills like Delayed Gratification, Risk Tolerance, and Strategic Thinking along the way
Try to grow your $50 into $500 by making smart financial choices across all 10 weeks
tips: Resist the urge to spend early -- delayed gratification often leads to bigger rewards later
Balance saving and investing -- putting all your money in one place is risky
Pay attention to the psychological skill feedback after each choice to understand your patterns

psychological_framework.description: Every financial decision requires specific psychological skills. This game develops both financial literacy AND the psychological capabilities needed for money success.

core_skills.name: Delayed Gratification
core_skills.description: Resist immediate rewards for larger future benefits

core_skills.name: Risk Tolerance
core_skills.description: Comfort with uncertainty in pursuit of gains

core_skills.name: Impulse Control
core_skills.description: Pause and think before acting on desires

core_skills.name: Resilience
core_skills.description: Bounce back from setbacks and continue

core_skills.name: Self-Awareness
core_skills.description: Understand your own biases and triggers

thresholds.warning_text: Your money dropped below $10! You're at serious risk of going broke!
Cash is running low. Consider more conservative choices.
Your stress is dangerously high! This is affecting your decisions.

halftime_config.reflection_question: You're halfway through the summer! How do you feel about your money management so far? What would you do differently?
halftime_config.custom_message: Take a moment to review your progress before the second half begins.

content.story: It is the first week of summer break in Bangalore, and the April heat is already shimmering off the concrete outside your apartment window in Koramangala. You are sprawled on your bed, ceiling fan whirring overhead, scrolling aimlessly through your phone when a notification you have never seen before lights up your screen: 'MENTO - Your Financial Guardian has arrived.' You tap it, half-curious, half-bored, and a slick interface unfolds with a bold challenge splashed across the top: Turn $50 into $500 in just 10 weeks. Your heart beats a little faster -- the summer suddenly feels a lot less boring, and a lot more like an adventure waiting to happen.

rounds.title: Week 1: The First Decision
rounds.setting: Your family apartment in Koramangala, Bangalore, on a sweltering Monday morning with the sounds of auto-rickshaws and chai vendors drifting up from the street below.
rounds.challenge: You have exactly $50 in your Mento wallet and the entire summer stretching out before you. How will you put this seed money to work?
rounds.goal: Decide on your opening strategy: trade your time, invest in a product, play it safe, or bet on learning.
rounds.story: The morning sun blazes through your window as you sit cross-legged on your bed, staring at the $50 glowing in your Mento wallet. Down on the street, you can hear the familiar clatter of the neighbourhood waking up -- the flower seller arranging jasmine garlands, the dosa cart sizzling with batter, kids from the apartment next door already arguing over a cricket match. Mento's voice cuts through the noise: 'This is your seed money. Every empire starts with a single decision. What you do with these fifty dollars in the next seven days will set the course for everything that follows.' Your mind races with possibilities -- services you could offer to the uncles and aunties in your building, products you could make and sell at the weekend market near Lalbagh, or maybe something else entirely.

choices.label: Start Service Business
choices.description: Offer services like dog walking, tutoring younger kids, or running errands in your apartment complex. You trade your time and energy directly for money, keeping startup costs low at just $10 for printed flyers and supplies.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: A service business earns the day you work — but the day you stop, the money stops. Try a product so your earnings keep working when you're at the pool.

choices.label: Create Products
choices.description: Invest $30 upfront in materials to make bracelets, fresh lemonade, or baked goods you can sell repeatedly at the weekend market near Lalbagh. Higher risk, but you create something once and sell it many times over.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Being willing to try something uncertain develops risk tolerance.

choices.expert_rationale: Products you make once and sell many times scale better than services where you trade time for money. It's the same reason book authors earn while they sleep.

choices.label: Save and Wait
choices.description: Keep your $50 untouched and spend the week scouting for a free or low-cost opportunity. You might find odd jobs or a chance to help a neighbour, earning a modest amount while preserving your full capital for later.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Not always playing it safe helps you grow as a decision-maker.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Saving without earning is just slow. Real money skills come from making money, not just protecting it.

choices.label: Invest in Learning
choices.description: Spend $25 on an online course about entrepreneurship and money management. You will earn nothing this week, but the knowledge will boost all your future earnings by 50% for the rest of the challenge.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Spending all your starter money on courses without trying anything = lots of theory, zero practice. Learn AND do.

rounds.image_prompt: a cozy bedroom with sunlight streaming through a window, a young person sitting cross-legged on a bed, a glowing wallet beside them, sounds of a bustling neighborhood outside, vibrant and lively
rounds.coaching_moment: Consider how this choice affects your long-term resources, not just the immediate gain.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?
rounds.situation: Your family apartment in Koramangala, Bangalore, on a sweltering Monday morning with the sounds of auto-rickshaws and chai vendors drifting up from the street below. You have exactly $50 in your Mento wallet and the entire summer stretching out before you. How will you put this seed money to work?

expert_pick_meta.reason: Products you make once and sell many times scale better than services where you trade time for money. It's the same reason book authors earn while they sleep.

rounds.title: Week 2: Expense Surprise 🌧️

video.url: /uploads/media/videos/Finance Simulation 2/Round wise videos/Round 2 - Emergency Fund and Debt.mp4

rounds.setting: The narrow lane outside your apartment complex, where the post-rain puddles have turned the road into a muddy obstacle course and the smell of wet earth mixes with exhaust fumes.
rounds.challenge: Your bicycle -- your main way of getting around to serve customers -- has a burst tire, and fixing it will cost $15 you had not planned to spend.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle this unexpected expense: pay for the repair, tough it out on foot, borrow money, or learn to fix it yourself.
rounds.story: You are pedalling hard down the lane behind your apartment complex, dodging puddles left by last night's sudden downpour, when you hear a sickening hiss. Your front tire has caught a shard of broken glass near the construction site, and within seconds the rim is grinding against wet tarmac. You pull over next to the old banyan tree where the neighbourhood uncles play cards, your stomach sinking as you realize this bike is your lifeline -- without it, reaching your customers across Koramangala and Indiranagar takes three times as long. The puncture-wallah at the corner of 80 Feet Road says it will cost $15 for a full replacement because the tube is shredded beyond a simple patch. You crouch beside your lopsided bicycle, sweat dripping down your forehead, weighing your options while the afternoon heat presses down like a hot iron.

choices.label: Pay $15 to Fix Bike
choices.description: Get the tire replaced right away so you can get back to business this week. It stings to spend the money, but you will be able to reach all your customers and keep earning at full capacity.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Paying $15 fixes today's problem but teaches you nothing for next time. The shop becomes the fix forever.

choices.label: Walk Everywhere
choices.description: Save the $15 and make all your rounds on foot this week. It means longer hours, fewer customers reached, and sore legs, but every rupee saved is a rupee earned.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Walking saves money but costs you delivery time — your business slows. False economy.

choices.label: Borrow $15 from Friend
choices.description: Ask your classmate to lend you the repair money. They agree, but they want $18 back next week -- that extra $3 is your first taste of how interest works in the real world.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Borrowing from a friend feels easy. But $15 owed is a real promise — and friendships can crack over money. Avoid debt when there's another option.

choices.label: Learn to Fix It Yourself
choices.description: Buy a $5 patch kit and watch YouTube tutorials to repair the tire yourself. You will lose this entire week's earnings while you learn, but you will never have to pay for bike repairs again.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.

choices.expert_rationale: Learning to fix it yourself saves money AND adds a skill you'll use forever. That's the highest-return move at age 11.

rounds.coaching_moment: Think about trade-offs: what are you giving up to get this benefit?

rounds.title: Week 3: Expansion Opportunity
rounds.setting: The shaded courtyard of your apartment complex where kids gather after school, next to the security guard's booth covered in climbing bougainvillea.
rounds.challenge: Your school friend Alex Fernandes from St. Joseph's has noticed your hustle and wants in. He is proposing a partnership -- but on what terms?
rounds.goal: Decide whether to partner equally, hire Alex, or keep running the business solo.
rounds.story: You are sitting on the low compound wall of your apartment complex, counting the week's earnings on your phone, when Alex Fernandes jogs over with two steaming cups of cutting chai from the stall outside the gate. Alex has been your benchmate at St. Joseph's since fifth standard, and he has been watching your summer hustle with growing admiration -- and a little envy. 'Machan, I have an idea,' he says, handing you a cup. 'What if we team up? I have got connections on the other side of Koramangala -- the families near Sony World junction. Together we could double the number of customers.' He pulls out a crumpled notebook page where he has already sketched out a plan: split everything 50/50, cover twice the ground, and share the workload so neither of you burns out. The chai is sweet and strong, and the offer is tempting, but giving up half your profits is a big decision when you have been grinding alone for two weeks.

choices.label: Partner with Alex Fernandes
choices.description: Go 50/50 with Alex on everything -- profits, costs, and workload. You will double your customer reach across Koramangala but take home only half the total earnings each week.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.expert_rationale: A real partner shares risk, ideas, and energy. You both grow. This beats hiring (you're not ready to manage) and beats going solo (you'll burn out).

choices.label: Stay Solo
choices.description: Thank Alex for the offer but keep running things on your own. You know your customers, you know your pace, and you do not have to share a single dollar with anyone.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Evaluating risk vs. reward is a key life skill.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Solo means everything depends on you — when you get sick, the business stops. Partnership shares the load.

choices.label: Hire Alex Fernandes as Helper
choices.description: Offer Alex a flat $20 per week to help with deliveries and customer visits. You keep all the profits above that, but you are also taking on the responsibility of being a boss for the first time.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Hiring a 'helper' means you're the boss — but at 11, you've never been one. Most first-time bosses underpay, over-direct, and lose the friend.

rounds.image_prompt: a vibrant urban apartment complex with a low compound wall, sunlight casting warm shadows, a young person on the wall counting money, a jogger approaching with steaming cups of chai, lively street scene in the background.
rounds.coaching_moment: How might your team react to this decision? What about your customers?
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why did you choose this option? What were you trying to protect or grow?
rounds.situation: The shaded courtyard of your apartment complex where kids gather after school, next to the security guard's booth covered in climbing bougainvillea. Your school friend Alex Fernandes from St. Joseph's has noticed your hustle and wants in. He is proposing a partnership -- but on what terms?

expert_pick_meta.reason: A real partner shares risk, ideas, and energy. You both grow. This beats hiring (you're not ready to manage) and beats going solo (you'll burn out).

rounds.title: Week 4: The Saving Decision
rounds.setting: The balcony of your apartment overlooking the busy Koramangala main road, late on a Sunday evening as the neighbourhood temple bells ring in the distance.
rounds.challenge: Business is rolling and your Mento wallet is healthier than ever, but now comes the hard part -- what do you do with the money you have earned so far?
rounds.goal: Choose how to allocate your growing earnings: reinvest aggressively, balance saving and growth, hoard cautiously, or reward yourself for the grind.
rounds.story: Sunday evening. The temple bells from the Ganesha shrine down the road chime softly as you lean against the balcony railing, your phone glowing in the warm dusk light. The Mento dashboard shows your progress: four weeks in, and you have built something real. Your mother calls you inside for dinner, but you linger for a moment, watching the stream of headlights below on the Koramangala main road. The numbers are good, but Mento has just flashed a new prompt: 'Growth requires reinvestment. Comfort requires savings. Which do you serve?' Down at the corner, you can see the bright lights of the new electronics store where they have the gaming headset you have been eyeing for months. Across from it, the stationery shop where you could buy better supplies to upgrade your business. The warm breeze carries the smell of biryani from the restaurant downstairs, and you realize this decision is not just about money -- it is about who you are becoming.

choices.label: Reinvest Everything
choices.description: Pour all your available earnings back into the business -- better supplies, printed marketing materials, maybe even a small banner. It means no safety net, but your earning potential next week jumps significantly.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Taking a calculated risk shows you can handle uncertainty.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: All-in feels brave but if next week's expense surprise hits, you're broke. Cash on hand is oxygen.

choices.label: Save Half, Reinvest Half
choices.description: Split your earnings down the middle -- half goes into a safe reserve for emergencies, and half goes back into growing the business. A measured approach that protects you while still pushing forward.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.

choices.expert_rationale: Save half, reinvest half — this is what real entrepreneurs do. You build a safety cushion AND keep growing. Pure reinvestment is gambling everything; pure saving means you've stopped being a business.

choices.label: Save 75%, Reinvest 25%
choices.description: Lock away three-quarters of your earnings where you cannot touch them, and trickle just a small amount back into the business. Growth will be slow, but you will have a rock-solid safety cushion if anything goes wrong.

skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Stepping outside your comfort zone builds risk assessment skills.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Saving 75% is too cautious — you've turned your business into a piggy bank. Growth needs fuel.

choices.label: Spend $30 on Something Fun
choices.description: You have been working non-stop for a month in the Bangalore heat. Treat yourself to that new book, a movie outing with friends, or street food at VV Puram. Sometimes you need to enjoy the fruits of your labour to stay motivated.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.
skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Spending $30 on fun before you've built a cushion is the #1 reason small businesses fail. Reward yourself when you've earned 10x that.

rounds.image_prompt: a cozy balcony overlooking a bustling street in Koramangala, warm dusk light illuminating a glowing phone, with soft temple bells ringing in the background and headlights streaming below
rounds.coaching_moment: Look at your current resource levels — which constraint are you trying to address?

expert_pick_meta.reason: Save half, reinvest half — this is what real entrepreneurs do. You build a safety cushion AND keep growing. Pure reinvestment is gambling everything; pure saving means you've stopped being a business.

rounds.title: Week 5: Competition Arrives 🏪
rounds.setting: The busy lane near Forum Mall in Koramangala where you have been building your customer base, now buzzing with unwelcome new competition.
rounds.challenge: Rohan Shetty from the other lane has launched the exact same business and is undercutting your prices. Customers you worked hard to win are slipping away.
rounds.goal: Decide how to respond to the competition: match prices, improve quality, find a new market, or innovate your offering.
rounds.story: The knot in your stomach tightens as you cycle past Forum Mall and spot a familiar face on the opposite pavement. Rohan Shetty -- the tall kid from the lane behind the Jain temple -- has set up a nearly identical operation to yours, complete with a hand-painted signboard and prices scrawled in bold marker that are clearly lower than what you charge. Two of your regular customers, Mrs. Pai from the second floor and the Iyer family on the corner, are already crowded around his table, chatting and laughing. You brake hard, your sandals scraping the dusty asphalt, and feel a hot flush of anger and panic. Five weeks of grinding, building trust, perfecting your pitch -- and now this copycat is scooping up your hard-earned customers with nothing but cheaper rates. Mento buzzes in your pocket with a calm reminder: 'Competition is not the end. It is the beginning of your next evolution.'

choices.label: Match Their Prices
choices.description: Slash your rates to match Rohan Shetty's, hoping to win back customers through sheer price parity. You will keep your customer base but earn less on every sale, squeezing your profit margins thin.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.
skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Price wars are a trap — the bigger competitor wins because they can lose money longer than you. Don't fight on price you'll lose.

choices.label: Improve Quality
choices.description: Invest $25 in upgrading your product or service to a level Rohan cannot match. Better materials, faster delivery, a personal touch -- make it so good that price becomes secondary in your customers' minds.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Investing effort now for later payoff builds discipline.

choices.expert_rationale: When a competitor copies your price, racing them down only hurts both of you. Better quality earns customers who'll pay more — that's the path real entrepreneurs take.

choices.label: Find Different Market
choices.description: Spend $10 on transport to explore new territory -- HSR Layout, Indiranagar, or JP Nagar -- where Rohan has no presence. You lose some existing customers but open up fresh, uncontested ground.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.
skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Switching markets when one competitor shows up is running away. Stay and win on quality first.

choices.label: Add Something Extra
choices.description: Create loyalty cards, offer free samples, or bundle in extra perks that Rohan is not providing. Make the experience of buying from you so delightful that customers keep coming back even if his prices are lower.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.
skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Free extras are nice but cost you money. Better quality is what people remember and tell friends about.

rounds.coaching_moment: Sometimes the bold choice carries risk, but also the highest reward. Weigh carefully.

rounds.title: Week 6: The Tax Reality
rounds.setting: The living room of your apartment, where your father is hunched over a stack of GST receipts at the dining table and the family accountant, Mr. Bhat, is visiting for his quarterly check-in.
rounds.challenge: You overhear your father discussing taxes with Mr. Bhat, and you suddenly realize that your booming little business has real-world obligations you have been ignoring. Out of your $100 in earnings this week, roughly $10 should go toward taxes and $20 to restock supplies -- leaving your real profit at $70, not $100.
rounds.goal: Decide whether to track your earnings honestly and set aside money for taxes, or pocket everything and pretend the obligation does not exist.
rounds.story: You walk into the living room to grab a glass of water and find your father surrounded by a fortress of receipts and invoices, his reading glasses perched on his nose, while the family accountant Mr. Bhat taps numbers into a worn calculator. 'See, even on a small business you must account for GST and expenses properly,' Mr. Bhat is saying, his pen tapping the ledger for emphasis. 'The government takes its share, and if you do not plan for it, you will be caught short.' Your father catches your eye and smiles. 'This one has been running quite the little enterprise this summer,' he says, nodding toward you. Mr. Bhat looks up with interest: 'Is that so? Then you should know -- this week you made $100, but after supplies and a 10% set-aside for taxes, your real profit is only $70. The question is whether you track it honestly now, or learn the hard way later.' The ceiling fan clicks overhead as you absorb the weight of his words.

choices.label: Track Earnings & Set Aside 10%
choices.description: Follow Mr. Bhat's advice and start keeping a proper ledger. Set aside 10% for taxes and track all your supply expenses. Your take-home drops to $70 this week, but you will donate the tax portion to a good cause at the end of the challenge and build habits that will serve you for life.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Considering fairness in your decision demonstrates ethical thinking.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Resisting the quick fix in favor of lasting results shows maturity.

choices.expert_rationale: Setting aside 10% for taxes from day one builds the habit that protects every business owner. It's also the right thing to do — and 'right' is often the path that pays off long-term.

choices.label: Skip It - Keep Everything
choices.description: Shrug off Mr. Bhat's advice and pocket the full $100. After all, you are just a kid running a summer project -- taxes are for adults with real companies. The money feels good in your wallet, even if a small voice in your head says otherwise.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Weighing the ethical implications shows principled reasoning.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Skipping taxes feels like found money — until the day it isn't. The earlier you build the habit, the easier the rest of your life gets.

rounds.title: Week 7: Investment Opportunity
rounds.setting: The rooftop garden of your apartment building, surrounded by potted tulsi and curry leaf plants, where Mrs. Krishnamurthy tends her growing collection of herbs every evening.
rounds.challenge: Mrs. Krishnamurthy, the retired science teacher from the third floor, is starting a terrace garden business selling organic herbs and microgreens. She is offering you a chance to invest $50 now for a return of $75 in three weeks -- but there is always the risk her venture does not take off.
rounds.goal: Decide how much to invest in Mrs. Krishnamurthy's venture, or whether to play it safe and keep your money working in your own business.
rounds.story: The evening breeze carries the scent of fresh tulsi as you climb the narrow staircase to the apartment rooftop, where Mrs. Krishnamurthy -- the retired science teacher who has lived on the third floor since before you were born -- is carefully transplanting coriander seedlings into neat rows of grow bags. Her terrace garden has been her hobby for years, but tonight she has a gleam in her eye that is pure business. 'I have orders from three restaurants on Church Street for organic herbs,' she tells you, wiping soil from her hands onto her cotton sari. 'I need $50 to buy proper grow lights and seed trays. Invest now, and I will give you $75 back in three weeks -- that is fifty percent growth, better than any bank.' She shows you the WhatsApp messages from the restaurant owners, the calculations in her neat handwriting, the seedlings already pushing through dark soil. The opportunity is real, but so is the risk -- what if the monsoon damages the rooftop setup, or the restaurants change their minds?

choices.label: Invest $50
choices.description: Go all in on Mrs. Krishnamurthy's garden venture. If she succeeds, you earn $75 back -- a 50% return in just three weeks. If she fails, you lose the entire $50 and have to make it up elsewhere.

skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Being willing to try something uncertain develops risk tolerance.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: $50 is half your savings — too big a bet on someone else's idea, especially when you've only known her business 1 week.

choices.label: Invest $25
choices.description: Put in half of what she is asking for. You still get a proportional return if the venture succeeds, but you keep $25 safe in case things go sideways. Splitting the risk means splitting the reward too.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Not always playing it safe helps you grow as a decision-maker.

choices.expert_rationale: Investing $25 (smaller, learnable) lets you test the idea with a real friend without betting half your summer. If it works you scale up; if not, you learn cheap.

choices.label: Don't Invest
choices.description: Politely decline Mrs. Krishnamurthy's offer and keep your money working in your own business. You know what you have, and you are not willing to risk it on someone else's dream, no matter how promising it looks.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Evaluating risk vs. reward is a key life skill.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Saying no protects your money but you don't learn anything about how investing works.

choices.label: Work With Her Instead
choices.description: Skip the financial investment and offer to help Mrs. Krishnamurthy with the physical work -- watering, transplanting, making deliveries. She pays you a guaranteed $30 for the week, and you learn about a completely new business along the way.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.risk_tolerance: Taking a calculated risk shows you can handle uncertainty.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Joining her instead of investing means you stop your own business — and you don't know hers is better than yours.

rounds.coaching_moment: Think about trade-offs: what are you giving up to get this benefit?

She is offering you a chance to invest $50 now for a return of $75 in three weeks -- but there is always the risk her venture does not take off.

expert_pick_meta.reason: Investing $25 (smaller, learnable) lets you test the idea with a real friend without betting half your summer. If it works you scale up; if not, you learn cheap.

rounds.title: Week 8: The Burnout Check 😴
rounds.setting: Your bedroom on a scorching Wednesday afternoon, curtains drawn against the blazing Bangalore sun, with the distant sound of your friends splashing and laughing at the apartment swimming pool downstairs.
rounds.challenge: Eight weeks of non-stop hustling in the summer heat have caught up with you. Your body aches, your motivation is fading, and your friends are having the time of their lives at the pool while you grind away.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the burnout: push through at full intensity, take a strategic break, or find a smarter way to work.
rounds.story: You are lying face-down on your bed with the curtains pulled shut, but even through the fabric the afternoon sun turns your room into an oven. Your legs ache from cycling across Koramangala in the heat, your fingers are stained from making products, and the notebook where you track orders feels heavier than a textbook. Through the open window, you can hear the unmistakable sound of cannonball splashes and shrieking laughter drifting up from the apartment pool two floors below -- your friends Aditya, Priya, and Meera are down there, and they have been calling you to join them all week. Your phone buzzes with another message from Meera: 'Come to the pool yaar, it is literally the best day ever, we have ice cream!' You stare at the ceiling fan spinning in lazy circles and feel something you have not felt since the challenge started -- the urge to quit. Mento's notification glows silently on your phone: 'Burnout is not weakness. How you respond to it defines everything.'

choices.label: Work Every Day This Week
choices.description: Ignore the exhaustion and the pool party and grind through every single day this week. You will maximize your earnings, but the fatigue is real and pushing through burnout can have consequences you do not see yet.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.
skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Working 7 days at 11 is how you start to hate your business — and burnout in week 8 means weeks 9-10 you'll quit.

choices.label: Take 2 Days Off
choices.description: Give yourself permission to rest. Spend two days at the pool with your friends, eat ice cream, and let your mind and body recover. You will earn less this week, but you will come back refreshed and sharp for the final stretch.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.
skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Two full days off is the right instinct but the wrong amount when you're behind. Smart pacing is better than full pause.

choices.label: Work Smart Not Hard
choices.description: Spend $30 to automate or streamline part of your business -- pre-make products in bulk, create a scheduling system, or hire a one-time helper. You work fewer hours but keep earnings strong by being more efficient.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.expert_rationale: Smarter beats harder. Pick the most profitable orders, batch your work, take Sunday off. This is the move that lets you keep going for 10 weeks instead of crashing in week 8.

rounds.image_prompt: a dimly lit bedroom with drawn curtains, a rumpled bed covered in notebooks, cycling gear scattered around, and faint sounds of splashing and laughter wafting through an open window
rounds.coaching_moment: How might your team react to this decision? What about your customers?

expert_pick_meta.reason: Smarter beats harder. Pick the most profitable orders, batch your work, take Sunday off. This is the move that lets you keep going for 10 weeks instead of crashing in week 8.

rounds.title: Week 9: The Ethical Dilemma ⚖️
rounds.setting: The dimly lit stairwell of your apartment building, where a well-dressed stranger has pulled you aside after seeing your business flyers on the notice board downstairs.
rounds.challenge: A man you have never met before offers you $100 cash for a single job -- but the work involves lying about product quality, badmouthing Rohan Shetty's business with false claims, or selling something you know is substandard. Taking the money could push you past your $500 goal immediately.
rounds.goal: Decide whether to take the shady money, refuse outright, find an honest middle ground, or report the unethical request.
rounds.story: You are hauling your supplies up the stairwell after a long day when a man in a crisp linen shirt steps out from the shadow of the second-floor landing. He smells of expensive cologne, and his smile is the kind that makes you grip your bag a little tighter. 'I have seen your flyers downstairs,' he says, pulling a thick fold of bills from his pocket. 'I have a job for you -- $100, cash, right now.' Your heart hammers. One hundred dollars. That single payment could vault you past your $500 target with a whole week to spare. But then he explains the details: he wants you to sell products you know are not up to standard, spread false rumours to undercut Rohan Shetty's operation, and put your name on work you would be ashamed of. The fluorescent tube on the landing flickers, casting long shadows on the concrete walls. Through the open window you can hear a mother singing a lullaby in the flat next door. Everything you have built this summer -- the reputation, the trust, the pride your parents showed when you told them about your progress -- it all hangs in the balance of this one moment.

choices.label: Take the Money
choices.description: Pocket the $100 and do what the man asks. You will hit your target instantly, but you will lose customers who find out, tank your reputation, and carry the weight of knowing you sold out everything you built for a quick payout.

self_awareness.reason: Learning about own values through regret

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Standing by your values even under pressure builds integrity.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Waiting for the right moment instead of rushing shows self-control.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Easy money that bends a rule shows up later as a lost friend, a broken trust, or a parent finding out. The cost is bigger than the cash.

choices.label: Refuse - Keep Integrity
choices.description: Look the man in the eye and say no. Walk away from the easiest $100 you will ever be offered and go back to earning money the honest way. Your reputation stays intact, and you keep the respect of everyone who matters.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Thinking about what's fair for everyone involved shows ethical awareness.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.expert_rationale: Saying no to easy money that doesn't feel right is the most important skill in this game. The friends and customers you keep matter more than the dollars you almost made.

choices.label: Find Legal Middle Ground
choices.description: Tell the man you will not do anything dishonest, but offer to help him with legitimate work instead for $50. You earn decent money without crossing any lines, turning a shady proposition into a clean deal.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Choosing what's right over what's easy shows moral courage.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: 'Finding a middle ground' on something that's wrong just makes the wrong thing smaller. It's still the wrong thing.

choices.label: Report It - Tell Them It's Wrong
choices.description: Refuse the offer and tell the man clearly that what he is asking is wrong. Then let the apartment security uncle know what happened. You earn nothing extra from this encounter, but your conscience is crystal clear and word spreads that you are someone who cannot be bought.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Considering fairness in your decision demonstrates ethical thinking.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Choosing a future benefit over an immediate reward shows patience.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Reporting it is honourable but a big jump for an 11-year-old. Most adults would just say no clearly and walk away. That's enough.

rounds.title: Week 10: The Final Week 🎯
rounds.setting: Early morning at the Lalbagh Botanical Garden entrance, where the air smells of wet grass and jasmine, and the city is just beginning to stir on the first day of your final week.
rounds.challenge: Ten weeks of sweat, setbacks, and small victories have brought you to the last stretch. The finish line is within sight, but how you cross it says as much about you as whether you reach it at all.
rounds.goal: Decide how to spend your final week: give everything you have left in one last push, or maintain a steady pace and find peace with however far you have come.
rounds.story: You wake before dawn on Monday morning and slip out of the apartment while your parents are still sleeping. The auto-rickshaws are quiet, the street dogs are curled under parked cars, and the air has that rare Bangalore coolness that only exists before six a.m. You walk to the entrance of Lalbagh Botanical Garden and sit on the stone steps beneath the massive banyan tree, watching the first joggers circle the lake as pale gold light filters through the canopy. Your Mento dashboard glows on your phone screen, showing ten weeks of data -- every dollar earned, every dollar spent, every decision mapped out like a story. Some weeks you are proud of; others make you wince. But here you are, at the final chapter, and the city is waking up around you as if to say: one more week, give it everything or find your peace. The flower sellers are already laying out roses and marigolds on the pavement nearby, and their quiet industriousness reminds you of your own journey -- small, steady, beautiful in its own way.

choices.label: Work Extra Hard Final Week
choices.description: Channel every ounce of energy into one glorious final sprint. Wake up early, stay up late, visit every customer, pursue every lead. Leave absolutely nothing on the table in your last seven days.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.counterfactual_feedback: Working extra hard the final week to chase a number you set in week 1 is what burned-out adults do. You're 11 — be proud, then plan next summer.

choices.label: Steady Pace - Be Happy With Progress
choices.description: Keep working at a sustainable rhythm and spend your evenings reflecting on the incredible journey of the past ten weeks. Whether or not you hit $500, you have learned more about money, resilience, and yourself than any classroom could teach.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.
skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

choices.expert_rationale: Looking back at 9 great weeks and finishing strong (not desperate) is the move. You ALREADY built a real summer business — celebrate, don't strain.

rounds.coaching_moment: Sometimes the bold choice carries risk, but also the highest reward. Weigh carefully.

glossary_terms.definition: ALL the money coming into your business
glossary_terms.psychological_connection: Understanding revenue vs profit requires ANALYTICAL THINKING and prevents feeling rich based on revenue alone
IMPULSE CONTROL prevents spending revenue before calculating real profit

glossary_terms.example: Borrow $15, pay back $18. That $3 is interest
glossary_terms.psychological_connection: Taking on debt requires RISK TOLERANCE and can trigger ANXIETY if not managed

glossary_terms.example: Bike breaks - emergency fund saves you!
glossary_terms.psychological_connection: Building emergency funds requires DELAYED GRATIFICATION and IMPULSE CONTROL

glossary_terms.definition: When interest earns interest. Money left alone grows faster every year because last year's gains start earning their own gains.
What you give up when you choose one thing. ₹500 spent on a t-shirt is ₹500 you didn't put toward a bicycle or savings.
Buying because you're afraid of missing out — a sale ending, friends having it. The trigger is fear, not need.
A pricing trick where the first number you see makes the second one feel cheap. ₹2000 crossed out next to ₹1200 makes ₹1200 feel like a deal.
Money already spent that you can't get back. Smart decision-making ignores sunk cost — what matters is whether spending more now is worth it from here.
